newsitem.title: USA: Mexico vows anti-drug step before Clinton visit.
newsitem.headline: Mexico vows anti-drug step before Clinton visit.

text.p: Mexico's President Ernesto Zedillo said on Tuesday he was planning a "radical" new step in the war on drugs as Latin American and Caribbean leaders met in a forum to seek a joint agenda with the United States for the 21st century.

Addressing one of the key topics of the two-day meeting, called by former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, Zedillo gave no details but said in a speech that the "radical and surprising step" against narcotics would come in a few days.
U.S. President Bill Clinton begins his first trip to Latin America by visiting Mexico for three days beginning on May 5.
A Zedillo aide said the measure would likely include abolishing the National Institute for Combating Drugs (INCD), Mexico's equivalent of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.

The head of INCD was arrested this year on drug corruption charges in a major embarrassment for Zedillo and for U.S. drug czar Gen. Barry McCaffrey, who had praised the integrity of the now-jailed Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo.

"The INCD is gone," the aide said, although he had no details on what would replace it. Media reports have said Mexico was working closely with the United States on setting up a new anti-narcotics agency.

Latin American and Caribbean leaders at the meeting accused the United States of arrogance in its war on drugs, especially the annual "certification" process wherein the U.S. government grades other countries' anti-narcotics efforts.

Zedillo, while acknowledging drug corruption in Mexico, demanded respect for the sovereignty of other nations. "The United States has never given Mexico an ultimatum on anything, at least during my government," he said. "If that were to happen my government would reject it radically."

The leaders also accused the United States of dragging its feet on expanding free trade in Latin America and the Caribbean and U.S. special envoy to the Americas Thomas "Mack" McLarty pledged late on Monday that Clinton's trip -- he will also visit Central America and the Caribbean -- would bring renewed efforts to boost free trade beyond North American Free Trade Agreement partners Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Inter American Development Bank President Enrique Iglesias, a Uruguayan, said strong growth in Latin America would make the Western Hemisphere "a major engine of growth for the whole world" in the next century. "In 2010 we will be the first area for exports of the United States," he said.

Latin American economies would grow by an average 4.5 percent this year and 5.0 percent next year amid falling inflation, he said, while production of goods and services would grow from $1.5 trillion now to $1.7 trillion by the end of the century.

Growth, fuelled by free trade, was necessary to help the 200 million people in the region now living below the poverty line -- out of a total population of 460 million -- to improve their standard of living, he said. "This is not a Biblical curse," he said. "Poverty can be addressed and can be solved."

Jamaican Prime Minister P.J. Patterson demanded that the Caribbean not be left out of free trade efforts, saying any new U.S. trade legislation must act as "a gateway to NAFTA." He said exclusion from the benefits of NAFTA had hit the area's economy hard, causing investment to dry up and thousands of jobs to be lost.
